analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more employees to give workers 10 paid vacation days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, no committee action, and no vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act so employers with at least 15 employees must provide each eligible worker at least 10 days of paid vacation per year. Workers qualify after one year on the job and 1,250 hours worked, and must give 15 days' notice before taking the time. Employers with equally generous paid-leave policies are exempt. The Department of Labor would enforce complaints and run a public awareness campaign.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time and regular part-time workers at employers with 15 or more staff who currently get no paid vacation, or less than 10 days. Tipped workers would be paid at the federal minimum cash wage during vacation, and benefits like health insurance would continue while on leave.

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees at least 10 days of paid vacation per year for eligible employees at employers with 15 or more staff, usable in consecutive or nonconsecutive days.

Protects tipped workers by requiring that vacation pay be at the federal minimum cash wage rather than the lower tipped cash wage, and requires benefits and restoration to the same position on return.
Gives the Department of Labor enforcement authority, including unpaid vacation pay plus an equal amount in liquidated damages.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would pay wages and maintain benefits for 10 vacation days per eligible worker per year. Businesses whose existing paid-leave policies already meet the standard would owe nothing extra. Costs could be absorbed through prices, slower hiring, or reduced hours for workers near the eligibility line.

drawbacks.text: Vacation time that is not used within the year does not carry over, so employees who cannot schedule a vacation lose it.
The 15-day advance written notice requirement lets employers plan around, and potentially discourage, vacation requests.
Workers at businesses with fewer than 15 employees get nothing, and new workers must wait a full year before qualifying.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly workers who lack paid vacation, 10 guaranteed paid days is a substantial, concrete gain, enforced with double damages. The main honest costs fall on employers, likely passed to prices or margins; the design is relatively simple and close to the FMLA's eligibility thresholds, though the no-carryover rule and notice requirement are real limitations.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in June 2015 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on June 11, 2015, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No committee action, floor vote, or additional steps followed; the action history shows only introduction and referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers without paid vacation policies are better off, because they never faced the new 10-day mandate. Workers who lack paid vacation gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Never considered or reported the bill, leaving it without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

against.name: U.S. Senate
against.what_they_did: Took no floor action; no senator besides the sponsor signed on.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no other senator cosponsored, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill died in a committee controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (retail, food service, and other low-wage sectors)
industries.note: Would owe 10 paid days per eligible worker per year, a direct labor cost for businesses that currently offer no or little paid vacation.
Included among covered employers; most already provide generous paid leave and would be exempt under the existing-policy carve-out.
